newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Foreign investors eye Israeli bond market.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors eye Israeli bond market.

text.p: Foreign investors who have practically ignored Israel's bond market are now exploring opportunities there and some are poised to enter, market sources say.
"There has been a lot of interest by foreign investors in the Israeli bond market recently," said Nadine Baudot- Trajtenberg, head of international sales for the securities division of Bank Hapoalim.

"We have had a lot of enquiries by foreign investors into the bond market. They are studying the market. But quantities of money have not started flowing into the market yet," said Ilan Doron of Solid Financial Markets.
Market sources said J.P. Morgan, Lehman Brothers, Salomon Brothers and Banque Nationale de Paris have put out feelers about entering the market and some are waiting for the final go-ahead.

Some of the banks contacted by Reuters confirmed they were seriously looking at the bond market, but most preferred to remain unidentified saying they would make their activities public when they were ready.

"We have been following the market daily. We are looking to get involved in the foreign exchange market and the bond market in Israel," said a trader at one of the banks. "We are waiting for the green light from different departments in the bank."
He said the entry point would be T-bills, like the Makam short-term, zero-coupon unlinked certificates that the Bank of Israel issues to absorb liquidity.
"If we are happy with the way the market behaves, how easy it is to enter and get out, the liquidity of the market, then we will try the other areas," he said.

"The spotlight is suddenly on Israel's fixed income sector because the government has been accessing the international capital markets without guarantees, and companies have been doing the same," said an investment banker who said his institution was seriously looking to enter the bond market.

In July, Israel raised $172 million in the samurai market and over the last year has conducted offerings in both the Euro- and Yankees. The offerings were aimed at testing international debt markets ahead of the expiry of the U.S. loan guarantees against which Israel has borrowed overseas in recent years.
Foreign investors have been trading equities on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) since about 1994 and put some $494 million in stocks in the first half of this year.
But Bank of Israel figures show that foreign holdings in government bonds amounted to just $340 million at the end of April, less than one percent of the total traded in the TASE.
"Financial investors in the emerging market sectors first come to the equity market, then they move on to the bond market," Baudot-Trajtenberg said.
Some bond specialists, like Martina Ben-Shaul, of the international bond sales department at Societe General, remain skeptical that Israel's debt market will attract much interest.
"The market is still only a fraction of a small European bond market. We tell customers that before entering the Israeli bond market they need to look at it in a very detailed way," she said.
The value of bonds traded on the TASE at the end of July was 146.1 billion shekels ($41 billion) and average daily trading volume 190 million shekels, TASE figures show.
"The market is lacking liquidity and transparency and it is difficult to trade from the outside. There is no real market-making culture," said the trader for the investment bank.

Eyal Rosner, a trader for Bankers Trust in Tel Aviv, said foreigners are deterred by the prevalence inflation-linked bonds that are difficult to understand and by the trading system, in which each bond is traded once daily.
One way to overcome those problems is by setting up a local office, Rosner said. Bankers Trust, one of the few foreign players in the Israeli market, has been active for three years.
"We have an advantage because we are sitting in Tel Aviv and follow the market from here," Rosner said.
The TASE has said it will introduce continuous trading in the bond market by the end of next year.
